slides.text:
You know how pointers work. Now you decide when to use one. Go copies values on every assignment and call, and a pointer is how you share instead.

You will see what gets copied, how to choose a receiver and a parameter, and what a copy still shares.

A struct is copied whole when you assign it, pass it or return it. A pointer is copied too, but both copies lead to the same struct.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
b = copy of a
change b -> a unchanged

p = address of a
change via p -> a changed

slides.text:
A method is a function with a receiver, the value written before its name. Inside `Add`, `p` is the receiver, and `pos.Add(other)` calls it on `pos`.

The receiver is a value (`Point`) or a pointer (`*Wallet`). Methods get their own course later.

exercises.title: Return the new value
exercises.guide: A function that gets a struct by value changes only its copy. Return it to keep the change.

chunks.guide: A struct and a function that takes it by value.
This one changes its copy and hands it back.

notes.text: Gives the changed copy back to the caller

chunks.guide: The first call changes a copy that is thrown away. The caller keeps its balance.
Assign the returned copy back to the variable to keep the change.

exercises.title: Methods that return values
exercises.guide: Small types work well as values: a method returns a new one and never changes the receiver.

chunks.guide: A small struct with a method that builds a new Point from two.
Assign the result back to move the point.
Without the assignment, `pos` is untouched.

exercises.title: Add two points
exercises.guide: Return a new point from `Add`, then call it on `start`.

exercises.title: Copies in a chain
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `grow` works on a copy, so `a` stays 1. `grow(a)` is 2, and the outer `grow` receives that returned copy and makes it 3.

slides.text: Pick a pointer when the code must change the caller's data, or when the struct is big. A value receiver cannot change the caller's data: it works on a copy.

exercises.title: Pick the receiver
exercises.guide: Changing needs a pointer receiver. Give every method of the type the same kind.

chunks.guide: A struct and a method that only reads it. It takes a pointer too, so the type keeps one kind of receiver.
A method that changes the struct needs a pointer receiver, or it changes a copy.

notes.text: The method works on the caller's Wallet

chunks.guide: Call both on a variable. Go passes `&w` for you when needed.
A pointer calls the methods the same way.

notes.text: The method receives the pointer itself

exercises.title: Mutate through a pointer
exercises.guide: `Add` must change the caller's wallet. Fill the receiver type.

exercises.title: Why is it zero
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: A value receiver gets a copy of `m`, so `Set` changes the copy and `m.Level` stays 0.

exercises.title: Pick the parameter
exercises.guide: Reading a small struct takes a value. Changing the caller's struct takes a pointer.

chunks.guide: A small struct, and a function that only reads it, so it takes a value.
This one must change the caller's player, so it takes a pointer.

notes.text: Points at the caller's Player, not a copy

chunks.guide: Pass the address to the function that changes the struct.
The change is kept, and `show` still gets a copy to read.

exercises.title: Pass a big struct
exercises.guide: Pick the best parameter type for `update`.
options: *Report: avoids the copy, and the change is kept
Report: Go only copies the fields it changes
Report: the caller gets the change back anyway
exercises.explanation: A `Report` parameter is a full copy and the change would be lost. A pointer avoids the copy and updates the caller's struct.

exercises.title: One kind of receiver
exercises.guide: Pick the usual advice for the methods of `Stack`.
options: Keep both: values for reads, pointers for writes
Use value receivers on both methods
Use pointer receivers on both methods
exercises.explanation: When one method needs a pointer receiver, give the type pointer receivers everywhere. Mixed kinds make it unclear whether a copy or the original is used.

slides.text:
A copy of a struct copies each field. A field that is a pointer copies the address, so the two structs still share what it points to.

Sharing is fine when you want it. A type should also stay consistent: one kind of receiver for all its methods.

exercises.title: A copy keeps the pointer
exercises.guide: Copying a struct copies its pointer fields, not what they point to.

chunks.guide: A team holds a pointer to its lead.
`b` is a copy of `a`, so each has its own Name.
chunks.text:
a := Team{"core", &Person{"ana"}}
    b := a
    b.Name = "ops"
    fmt.Println(a.Name)

chunks.guide: The Lead field holds a pointer, and the copy holds the same address. Both teams share one Person.

notes.text: Same address, so one shared Person

exercises.title: Give the copy its own data
exercises.guide: Copy what the pointer points to, then point the new team at the copy.

chunks.guide: The same types as before.
Copy the team, then copy its lead.
Point `b` at the copy. Now a change through `b` stays in `b`.

exercises.title: Separate the book
exercises.guide: `other` must get its own book, so renaming it leaves `shelf` alone.

exercises.title: What the copy shares
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `Size` is copied, so `a.Size` stays 3. `Lead` is a copied pointer to the same Person, so the new name shows in `a` too.
